title: Vec Push and Pop
story: You're building an undo feature for a drawing app. Every action gets pushed onto a stack, and when the user presses undo, you pop the last action off. But what if there's nothing to undo? The Vec tells you.
why: `.pop()` returns `Option[T]` — forcing you to handle the 'empty stack' case explicitly instead of crashing on a null value.
analogy: A Vec with push and pop is like a stack of cafeteria trays. You add trays on top (push) and take trays from the top (pop). If you reach for a tray and the stack is empty, you get nothing — and the Option tells you 'None.' You never have to guess whether you grabbed something.
try_it: Push 5 numbers onto a Vec and pop 3 of them. Print each popped value. Then check the Vec's length before and after all the operations. What value does the FIRST pop return? Try using `if let Some(val) = stack.pop() { ... }` instead of match — it's a shorter way to handle the Option.
tips: `.pop()` always removes from the END — it's Last-In-First-Out (LIFO), like a stack of plates
Always match on `.pop()` — the compiler won't let you ignore the `None` case
After popping N times from a Vec with N items, `.len()` will be 0
common_mistakes: Assuming `.pop()` returns the value directly: it returns `Option[T]`, so you MUST handle the None case
Thinking pop removes from the front — it removes from the back, opposite of what you might expect
Not checking `.len()` before popping if you want to avoid the None case entirely
